newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants Aerospatiale in public sector - paper.
newsitem.headline: France wants Aerospatiale in public sector - paper.

text.p: In the latest sign of its reluctance to part with state firms, France's Socialist-led government has said it hopes to keep aircraft company Aerospatiale in the public sector.

Defence Minister Alain Richard said in a newspaper interview on Thursday that France still wanted to link Aerospatiale with private warplane maker Dassault Aviation. But he hoped to keep the resulting company under state control.
"The government hopes to convince Dassault Aviation that this linking of forces can take place while keeping Aerospatiale in the public sector," the afternoon daily Le Monde quoted Richard as saying.

The decision may throw a planned merger of Dassault and Aerospatiale into doubt since Dassault Chairman Serge Dassault has said he would agree to merge his family firm with Aerospatiale only if the resulting company were privatised.

It may also hobble a much-needed restructuring of the European aircraft consortium Airbus Industrie which faces increasingly tough competition from arch-rival Boeing after the European Commission agreed in principle to approve its takeover of McDonnell Douglas.
Aerospatiale is one of the top partners in Airbus.

As recently as last month, Dassault repeated his demand for a privatisation of the company formed by any merger. "I remain in favour of a merger with Aerospatiale, provided this operation occurs simultaneously with privatisation," he told a news conference in June.
He said he could accept the state keeping a stake as big as 49 percent in the new merged entity.

A merger of the planemakers, part of a wider restructuring of the defence sector launched last year by President Jacques Chirac, is seen as essential for French companies to survive in the bitter battle for world markets with U.S. defence and aerospace giants.

The election of a Socialist-led coaliton in June has cast doubt on plans for Aerospatiale since the Socialists said during the election campaign that it favoured the merger but would halt the privatisation programme begun by the prior conservative government.
Richard said in the interview that France's overall strategy for the sector centred on a deeper European alliance in the civil aviation sector.

"Our European partners have already realised synergies between their civil and military aeronautic sectors and that is a target for France as well, but without losing sight of the final result, which is European," he said.
On July 11, the government cancelled the privatisation of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF in a move analysts said would slow the restructuring of the European defence sector.
The government said it would keep a "determining" stake in Thomson-CSF but said it was willing to see its shareholding drop below 50 percent.

Richard repeated the government's position that it would not completely sell off Thomson-CSF. The company would have no problem finding European partners despite speculation that private companies would be reluctant to link up with a company heavily influenced by the state, he said.
The previous government's aim was to restructure the French defence sector, creating a small group of powerful players able to play an important role in consolidation of the European industry.
The merger of Aerospatiale and Dassault would form a leading European aerospace group manufacturing combat planes, business jets, helicopters, missiles and satellites.
